profile.name: Turn
profile.tagline: A rotation of the body about the vertical axis in dance and gymnastics.
profile.insight: In ballet, a turn in the direction of the raised leg is termed 'en dehors,' while a turn in the opposite direction is 'en dedans,' a distinction that dictates the dancer's rotational path.
profile.profile: A turn is a fundamental rotation of the body around its vertical axis, serving as a core element in ballet, jazz, modern, and ballroom dance. Performers may execute these rotations while supported by one or both legs, or while airborne, utilizing techniques like spotting to maintain balance and direction. These movements range from simple pivots to complex, multi-rotational sequences like the 32 consecutive fouettés seen in classical ballet.
profile.profile_long:
In dance and gymnastics, a turn is defined as a rotation of the body about the vertical axis. While a complete 360-degree rotation is standard, turns can also be executed in quarter or half increments. The mechanics of a turn depend on the performer's support: they may be grounded on one or both legs, or they may be airborne. When supported by a single leg, that limb is designated the supporting leg, while the other is the free, raised, or working leg. During airborne turns, the first leg to leave the floor is the leading leg. 

Technique is paramount to the execution of a turn. Spotting is a critical method used to prevent dizziness and maintain orientation; the performer executes a rapid, periodic rotation of the head to fix their gaze on a single point, creating the impression that the head is always facing forward. This stability is essential for balance and for controlling the direction of travel in movements like the chaînés, a two-step turn performed repeatedly along a path. 

Different genres utilize specific terminology and variations. In ballet, the direction of the turn relative to the raised leg is categorized as either en dehors or en dedans. Ballroom dancing distinguishes between a natural turn, which is a clockwise revolution, and a reverse turn, which is counter-clockwise. A pivot, often used in Labanotation, describes a rotation without traveling, which can be performed on one or both feet. 

Specific named turns include the fouetté, which involves a whipping motion of the working leg to generate angular momentum, and the pirouette, a spin on one foot that is a staple of ballet and jazz. The axel and barrel roll involve airborne rotations, often seen in jazz and contemporary dance. The history of the turn is punctuated by technical feats, such as the 32 consecutive fouettés famously performed by Pierina Legnani in 1893, a standard now incorporated into the grand pas of Swan Lake. Jeanne Devereaux, an American prima ballerina, later recorded 16 triple fouettés, totaling 48 rotations. These movements continue to evolve across global dance traditions, serving as both technical challenges and expressive tools for performers.

sections.origins_and_history: The turn is a foundational element in classical ballet, jazz, modern, and ballroom dance. Its history is marked by technical milestones, such as the 32 consecutive fouettés first performed by Pierina Legnani in 1893.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Turns are executed by rotating the body around a vertical axis. Performers use spotting to maintain balance, fixing their gaze on a single point. Turns may begin from a plié or by stepping directly onto a relevé. The working leg may be held in various positions, such as retiré, attitude, or arabesque.
sections.notable_figures: Pierina Legnani, an Italian ballerina who first performed 32 consecutive fouettés in 1893. Jeanne Devereaux, an American prima ballerina who held the record for 16 triple fouettés.
sections.regional_variants: Ballet uses en dehors and en dedans. Ballroom dancing uses natural (clockwise) and reverse (counter-clockwise) turns.

basic_steps: Prepare in plié or fourth position.
Rise to relevé on the supporting leg.
Execute rotation while spotting the head.
Return to starting position or finish in a specific pose.
teaching.level_notes: Turns range from simple pivots to advanced multi-rotational sequences.

movement_profile.footwork: Supported by one or both legs; relevé or flat foot.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Positions vary; arms are often brought together away from the chest during turns like chaînés.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Turnout is used in ballet; torso pivots in illusions.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Can be performed in place (pivot) or traveling (chaînés, piqué).
movement_profile.partnering: Assistance may be provided in turns like the attitude turn.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Varies; chaînés are often performed at a fast tempo.

signature_moves.name: Chaînés

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Includes airborne turns like the axel and barrel roll.

claims.text: A turn is a rotation of the body about the vertical axis.
claims.quote: In dance and gymnastics, a turn is a rotation of the body about the vertical axis.

claims.text: Spotting is a technique used to fix the gaze on a single spot to prevent dizziness.
claims.quote: Spotting is a technique that is often used when executing turns, in which a performer executes a periodic, rapid rotation of the head that serves to fix the performer's gaze on a single spot

claims.text: In ballet, a turn in the direction of the raised leg is en dehors, while the opposite is en dedans.
claims.quote: In ballet, a turn in the direction of the raised leg is said to be en dehors whereas a turn in the opposite direction is en dedans.

claims.text: Pierina Legnani was the first to publicly perform 32 consecutive fouettés in 1893.
claims.quote: particular significance is attached to the successful completion of 32 consecutive fouettés, a feat first performed publicly by Italian ballerina Pierina Legnani in 1893

claims.text: Jeanne Devereaux held the record for 16 triple fouettés.
claims.quote: Jeanne Devereaux, an American prima ballerina in the first half of the 20th century, held the world record of 16 triple fouettés (48 total).

claims.text: Chaînés is a two-step turn executed repeatedly while traveling.
claims.quote: Chaînés (French, meaning "chain") is a type of two-step turn that is executed repeatedly while the performer travels along a line or curved (often circular or elliptical) path.
